newsitem.title: AZERBAIJAN: Karabakh vote wins Armenian approval, Azeri scorn.
newsitem.headline: Karabakh vote wins Armenian approval, Azeri scorn.

text.p: The self-styled leader of Azerbaijan's mainly ethnic Armenian enclave of Nagorno-Karabakh won a presidential election at the weekend that has stirred tensions between the Caucasian states.

Robert Kocharyan, who two years ago was elected president of the self-declared republic, won a new, five-year mandate with 86.11 percent of the vote, electoral officials said by telephone on Monday from the regional capital Stepanakert.

His rivals, former deputy parliament speaker Boris Arushayan and communist leader Grant Melkumyan, won 6.89 percent and 3.89 percent respectively. Turnout in Sunday's poll was 76 percent and local journalists said voting went smoothly.
Azerbaijan has condemned the vote as a ploy to entrench the capture of Nagorno-Karabakh by Armenia after a six-year war which cost more than 10,000 lives.

Several hundred of the Moslem Azeris displaced from the mainly Christian mountainous region in the fighting staged demonstrations in Azerbaijan at the weekend to protest at the vote and to call on Baku to take back Karabakh by force.
On Monday, President Haydar Aliyev called a closed meeting of regional and western ambassadors to discuss the election.
Western countries had joined Aliyev in urging the Karabakh leadership to cancel the vote, saying it could jeopardise peace talks involving Armenia and Azerbaijan.

On Friday, Armenia and Azerbaijan failed again to agree on resolving the conflict after talks in Helsinki and diplomats on both sides said an OSCE summit in Lisbon next month would probably not come any closer to a solution.
Karabakh, which declared independence in 1988, makes no secret of its desire to join Armenia. Azerbaijan refuses to consider anything more than autonomy for the region.
Supreme Court Chairman Khanlar Gadzhiev said Karabakh's Armenians would live to regret their independence declaration.
"The independence game will end in tears for the Armenians," he said.
Azeris interviewed on the streets of Baku feared the election would lead to more violence.
"I think that a new spiral of violence is unaviodable and will lead to more bloodshed," said Usnia Batayeva, a historian.
But in Armenia the vote was welcomed as a new step towards peace.
"We are happy that a president elected by the people will represent Karabakh's interests," Zhirayr Liparityan, Armenian President Levon Ter-Petrosyan's foreign policy aide, told a news conference.

Elmira Karapetyan, a 62-year-old former teacher from Karabakh said the result meant peace: "I lost two sons in that war. Now I elected the president, and I am happy that Robert Kocharyan is our president again. Robert Kocharyan means peace."
